title: CFA Ethics 47: Case - discovering misconduct where you work
subtitle: The order of the steps, the limits of any duty to report, and the point at which leaving is the right answer
whyItMatters: This is the situation where the standards demand less than people assume - they do not make you a whistleblower - but what they do demand is absolute, and many people miss it because they assume silence is neutral.
openingQuestion: You discover a colleague allocating profitable trades to a personal account and losing trades to client accounts. What is the first step?
openingOptions: Report it immediately to the regulator outside the firm
Raise it through internal channels and stop all participation in it
Speak directly to the affected clients
Gather more evidence over several months before acting
explanation: The CFA standards do not require a member to report externally - in many places the law restricts that, and a wrong accusation does real damage to the person accused. What they do require is two things: dissociate yourself from the violation, and raise the matter internally through the appropriate channel. Gathering more evidence over several months sounds prudent but is usually wrong, because the harm to clients keeps accumulating in the meantime and your silence gradually becomes consent. If the internal channel fails to act, the next steps are escalating to a higher level or to the board, and finally considering leaving the organisation.

summary.keyIdea: Between silence and public disclosure there is a mandatory step most people do not realise they have: dissociate and raise it internally, in writing.
summary.commonMistake: Treating silence and public whistleblowing as the only two options. There is a step in between, and it is the mandatory one.

application.title: If the internal channel does not act
application.message: Consider refusing to continue participating, and document everything. Leaving the organisation is the last option but it remains within scope.

sections.text: You discover a colleague or a superior doing something wrong. The CFA standards are very clear about two things you must do - and equally clear about what they do not demand.

items: Dissociate yourself from the violation: stop participating, stop signing, stop letting your name be attached to it.
Raise the matter internally through the appropriate channel - compliance, or a manager outside the chain involved.

sections.label: What the standards do NOT demand
sections.text: Reporting externally. In many places the law restricts that, and a wrong accusation does real damage to the person accused. The internal channel comes first.
Why "gather more evidence" is usually the wrong answer

It sounds prudent, but through those months of waiting the harm to clients keeps accumulating, and your silence gradually becomes consent. Dissociation is listed first precisely because it has no precondition - you can do it today, even without absolute certainty.

If the internal channel does not act, the next steps are escalating to a higher level, then to the board, and finally considering leaving the organisation. One thing to remember throughout: acting on instructions from a superior has never been a defence within the professional ethics framework.
The escalation ladder, and what ends each rung

sections.title: Four rungs, in this order
sections.subtitle: Each rung only opens once the previous one has been tried and failed

concepts.def: Stop participating, stop signing, stop letting your name be attached. This rung waits for nobody's agreement and does not depend on how the later rungs go - it is mandatory even if you decide to do nothing further.

concepts.vi: Nêu trong nội bộ qua kênh phù hợp
concepts.def: Your direct manager, compliance, or the designated internal channel. Preferably in writing - not to protect yourself, but because a spoken word is indistinguishable from never having raised it.

concepts.vi: Leo lên cấp cao hơn, rồi hội đồng quản trị
concepts.en: Escalate - when the previous rung fails
concepts.def: An organisation's silence is a datum, not an answer. If compliance takes the report and then does nothing for weeks, the duty has not been discharged.

concepts.en: Leave - when every channel is exhausted
concepts.def: Staying in an organisation you know to be in violation, after every internal channel has failed, gradually becomes condoning it. This is the point at which leaving is the standards' right answer, not a personal failure.

sections.label: Why gathering more evidence is usually the wrong answer
sections.text: It sounds prudent, and that is exactly the problem - it lets you do nothing while still feeling you are acting. Through those months of waiting the harm to clients keeps accumulating and your silence becomes harder and harder to distinguish from consent. The standards do not require you to be certain before raising it; investigating is compliance's job, and yours is to get it to the people with authority to investigate. A reasonable suspicion is enough to trigger rung two.

lines: You are not required to be the whistleblower.
But you are required not to be the accomplice.

diagram.label: Stop all participation in that conduct
Raise the matter through the appropriate internal channel
No action taken: escalate to a higher level
Still no action: consider leaving the organisation

realWorldExample.company: Why "I was only following instructions" is not an argument
realWorldExample.description: Standard I(A) states plainly that a member must dissociate from any violation, and that carries no exception for conduct originating with a superior. Continuing to perform your part in a process you know to be wrong is participation, even where you did not initiate it and gain nothing from it. This is also why the duty to dissociate is stated ahead of the duty to report: you may not yet know whom to report to, but you can always stop doing it.

quiz.question: Do the CFA standards require a member to report externally?
options: No, and they do not require anything else either
Yes, the regulator must be told as soon as it is discovered
Yes, if the harm exceeds a certain value threshold
No, but they require dissociation and raising it internally
quiz.explanation: In many places external reporting is restricted by law, and a wrong accusation does real damage - so the standard stops at the internal duty.

quiz.question: Why is "gathering more evidence over several months" usually wrong?
options: Because harm accumulates and silence becomes consent
Because evidence gathered individually has no legal weight
Because the rules require reporting within seven working days
Because the colleague may notice and destroy the evidence
quiz.explanation: It sounds prudent but is really delay, and the cost of the delay falls on clients rather than on you.

quiz.question: Which duty is stated first in the order of steps?
options: Reporting to the firm's compliance department
Dissociating yourself from the violation
Notifying the affected clients
Preserving the evidence of the violation
quiz.explanation: You may not yet know whom to report to, but you can always stop doing it - so this duty has no precondition at all.

quiz.question: How is "I was only following my manager's instructions" treated?
options: Not an argument - continuing to perform is participation
A mitigating factor if the instruction can be proved
A full defence - the person who ordered it is responsible
Accepted only if you gained nothing from the violation
quiz.explanation: Standard I(A) carries no exception for conduct originating with a superior - that is the entire meaning of the duty to dissociate.

quiz.question: What is the final step once every internal channel has failed to act?
options: Keep working, documenting it
Publish the matter in the media
Notify all the affected clients yourself
Consider leaving the organisation
quiz.explanation: Staying in an organisation you know to be in violation and unwilling to fix it returns you to the participation problem the first step dealt with.

keyTakeaways: The standards do not require external reporting, but they do require dissociation and raising it internally
Dissociation is stated first because it has no precondition at all
Drawn-out evidence gathering is delay - and the cost falls on clients
Following a superior's instructions is not a defence
When the internal channel is blocked: escalate, then consider leaving

practicePrompt.question: You reported it to compliance, they concluded there was no violation, but you still believe there was. What should you do?
options: Accept the conclusion, since the duty to report has been discharged
Dissociate from the related activity, and consider escalating
Report immediately to the external regulator
Gather more evidence yourself and report a second time
practicePrompt.explanation: The first option is where many people stop, and it is wrong on one specific point: the duty to dissociate does not depend on what compliance concluded. You have discharged the duty to report, but if you still believe the conduct is a violation, continuing to participate in it is still participation.
